definition: Baseload plants are generation units that are cheap to run but costly or physically risky to shut down, so they aim to operate continuously regardless of demand level.
core_idea: Hydro, nuclear, and coal plants are typically baseload because stopping them is expensive or operationally dangerous, so they bid low to stay online rather than risk being taken offline.
key_points: Hydro plants have no fuel cost and shutting down can risk flooding nearby communities.
Nuclear plants must actively spend money (control rods) to slow the reaction; without intervention it runs at max capacity, so slowing down is the costly action rather than running.
Coal plants are easier to shut down than hydro or nuclear but expensive to restart once fully cooled.
Baseload plants try to avoid being the marginal (price-setting) plant and will offer power at low prices specifically to stay online.
relationships: Baseload bidding behavior feeds into who sets the marginal price
trading_implications: Because baseload plants bid low to avoid shutting down, they are rarely the price-setting (marginal) unit in a region.
